extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies and owners/operators of fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating units (EGUs)
extracted.subtask_description: Final EPA emission-guideline preamble text specifying applicability, subcategories, BSER determinations (CCS, natural-gas co-firing), fuel-type definitions, exemptions, compliance dates, and cost/reasonableness metrics for existing fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated facility definition (applicability thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: A designated facility is any fossil fuel-fired electric utility steam generating unit (i.e., utility boiler or IGCC unit) that: (1) was in operation or had commenced construction on or before January 8, 2014; (2) serves a generator capable of selling greater than 25 MW to a utility power distribution system; and (3) has a base load rating greater than 260 GJ/h (250 MMBtu/h) heat input of fossil fuel (either alone or in combination with any other fuel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with implementing regulations, 'designated facility' refers to the single EGU affected by these emission guidelines; rationale parallels 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing vs. new/reconstructed/modified source applicability dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(a)(6) an 'existing source' is any stationary source other than a new source; the emission guidelines do not apply to steam generating units that are new after January 8, 2014 or reconstructed after June 18, 2014. A coal-fired unit that undertakes a modification after the date the proposal was published (May 23, 2023) would be considered 'new' and thus not subject to these emission guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units modified prior to the proposal publication remain existing and are subject to the guidelines; the preamble cross-references prior subpart TTTT discussions for rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions to requirement to establish standards under a state plan
rubrics_metrics.description: EGUs that may be excluded from the requirement to establish standards under a state plan include units falling into these categories: (1) units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT due to qualifying modification/reconstruction; (2) steam generating units subject to a federally enforceable permit limiting net-electric sales to one-third or less of potential electric output or ≤219,000 MWh annually and which have never exceeded that; (3) non-fossil fuel units (≥50% heat input from non-fossil fuel at base load rating) subject to permit limiting fossil fuel use to ≤10% of annual capacity factor; (4) combined heat and power units subject to a permit limiting annual net-electric sales to ≤219,000 MWh or the product of design efficiency and potential electric output; (5) units that serve a generator along with other affected EGU(s) where prorated effective generation capacity is ≤25 MW; (6) municipal waste combustor units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart Eb; (7) commercial/industrial solid waste incineration units subject to 40 CFR part 60, subpart CCCC; (8) EGUs deriving >50% heat input from an industrial process with no external useful output; (9) coal-fired steam generating units that have elected to permanently cease operation prior to January 1, 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some exemptions align with current 40 CFR 60.5509(b) exemptions; exemptions (2), (3), and (8) reflect finalized revisions to subpart TTTT; states should follow cross-referenced rationale in the preamble (section VIII.E.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of coal-fired units planning to cease operation before January 1, 2032
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is not addressing existing coal-fired steam generating units that demonstrate plans to permanently cease operation before January 1, 2032 in these emission guidelines and is not finalizing a BSER for such sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: these sources have limited emission reduction potential and capital-intensive controls (e.g., CCS) are unlikely to be cost-reasonable given short amortization periods; the exemption applies until the earlier of December 31, 2031 or the date the source demonstrates in the state plan that it plans to cease operation. If a source continues to operate past that date, it becomes subject to the guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-term subcategory BSER: 40% natural gas co-firing (for units ceasing by 2039)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sources demonstrating plans to permanently cease operating by January 1, 2039 (medium-term), the EPA is finalizing a BSER of 40 percent natural gas co-firing on a heat input basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is finalizing a compliance date of January 1, 2030 for natural gas co-firing; EPA assumes sources subject to a natural gas co-firing BSER can amortize costs for up to 9 years; EPA determined costs of 40% co-firing meet metrics for cost reasonableness for majority of capacity that operate more than 2 years after the Jan 1, 2030 implementation date (i.e., operate after Jan 1, 2032). States may use RULOF provisions to particularize standards where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term subcategory BSER: CCS with 90% capture
rubrics_metrics.description: For long-term coal-fired steam generating units (units that plan to operate at least seven years after the compliance date), the EPA is finalizing CCS with 90 percent capture of CO2 at the stack as the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance date for CCS is January 1, 2032; EPA concluded CCS achieves the largest emission reductions, is adequately demonstrated, is widely applicable, and is cost-reasonable for units that operate past January 1, 2039 (i.e., amortization period >7 years). If a particular source has fundamentally different CCS costs, states may consider RULOF alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of alternative controls for long-term units
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is not finalizing 40 percent natural gas co-firing, partial-CCS at lower capture rates (e.g., 30%), or HRI as the BSER for long-term coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: these alternatives either achieve substantially fewer unit-level reductions at greater cost (partial CCS), achieve markedly less reduction than CCS (co-firing), or have limited reductions and potential rebound effects (HRI). The IRC section 45Q tax credit may not apply to partial CCS, reducing cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finalized compliance dates for BSERs
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA finalized compliance dates as follows: January 1, 2030 for natural gas co-firing (medium-term units) and January 1, 2032 for CCS (long-term units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates reflect time needed for planning and installation; CCS was given additional time compared to the proposal to support planning and installation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel-type subcategory definitions (coal-fired, oil-fired, natural gas-fired)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions based on relative heat input contribution after December 31, 2029: a coal-fired steam generating unit burns coal for more than 10.0 percent of the average annual heat input during any continuous 3-calendar-year period after Dec 31, 2029, or more than 15.0 percent of annual heat input during any one calendar year after Dec 31, 2029, or retains capability to fire coal after Dec 31, 2029. An oil-fired unit is not coal-fired, no longer retains coal capability after Dec 31, 2029, and burns oil >10% on 3-year average or >15% in any one year; a natural gas-fired unit similarly is not coal- or oil-fired, no longer retains coal capability after Dec 31, 2029, and burns natural gas >10% on 3-year average or >15% in any one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPA based proposed definitions on 40 CFR part 63, subpart UUUUU and subpart TTTT fossil fuel definitions; being able to fire coal after Dec 31, 2029 preserves coal subcategory status unless capability is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule for fuel-type determination and constraints on conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final fuel-type subcategorization is based on the state of the source on the compliance date of January 1, 2030, and during any period thereafter (i.e., not a rolling pre-compliance lookback).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA rejected commenter proposals to make the determination rolling; constraints are intended to avoid perverse incentives to defer conversions that could undermine emission reductions. If a unit cannot fully convert by Jan 1, 2030, it will be treated as coal-fired, though the state may use RULOF provisions to particularize standards. If the state relies on source-controlled operating conditions as the basis for a less stringent standard or longer compliance schedule, those operating conditions must be enforceable requirements in the state plan (40 CFR 60.24a(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: IGCC units treated as coal-fired for subcategorization and BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing IGCC units are included in the coal-fired steam generating units subcategory; the BSER determinations for coal-fired units (co-firing for medium-term and CCS for long-term) apply to IGCC units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IGCC units gasify coal to produce syngas and may be suitable for pre-combustion CO2 capture (after water-gas shift) using amine-based or physical absorption capture processes; alternatively post-combustion capture can be applied. EPA therefore does not distinguish IGCC from other coal-fired EGUs for BSER purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope: non-contiguous areas excluded at this time
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is not finalizing emission guidelines for existing steam generating units in states and territories outside the contiguous U.S. (Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands) at this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: modeling focused on contiguous U.S., few coal-fired units outside contiguous 48 states meet applicability criteria, and proposed BSERs for non-continental oil-fired units would have yielded few emission reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination factors / criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In selecting BSERs the EPA evaluated technologies based on the degree of emission limitation achievable (emission reductions), whether the technology is adequately demonstrated, cost and cost reasonableness, non-air quality health and environmental impacts, energy requirements, and legal/precedential alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble describes weighing these factors together to finalize CCS as BSER for long-term units and natural gas co-firing for medium-term units; where a particular source's costs differ materially, RULOF may be used to particularize standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness metrics used for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's prior metrics for cost reasonableness are $18.50 per MWh of generation and $98 per ton of CO2 reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics were used to evaluate amortization period effects and to assess whether co-firing or CCS costs fall within previously deemed reasonable bounds for much of the fleet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amortization period thresholds for cost-reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's analysis finds CCS is cost-reasonable for amortization periods of more than 7 years (i.e., units operating after Jan 1, 2039). For natural gas co-firing, EPA determined costs meet reasonableness metrics for many units that operate more than 2 years after Jan 1, 2030 (i.e., operate after Jan 1, 2032). For units ceasing operation prior to Jan 1, 2032, CCS and 40% co-firing are generally not cost-reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example statistics: with a one-year amortization period almost no units meet both cost metrics for 40% co-firing; with a two-year amortization period, 18% of units can co-fire at 40% within cost bounds and 50% can co-fire at 20% within cost bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated standard for CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA determined CCS is 'adequately demonstrated' when all components (CO2 capture, CO2 transport, and CO2 sequestration) have been demonstrated concurrently and in concert, including commercial-scale applications and industrial uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes long-running solvent-based capture in industrial settings, thousands of miles of CO2 pipeline operation, tens of millions of tons of CO2 stored underground, at least 15 operating U.S. CCS projects and many more under construction, and commercial demonstrations at Boundary Dam Unit 3, Petra Nova, Quest, Shute Creek, and Great Plains Synfuels (with supporting metrics and capture volumes cited). Even if only individual components were demonstrated, EPA finds it reasonable that they can function together given engineering history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture-efficiency benchmark for CCS (90% capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes 90 percent CO2 capture at the stack as the capture-efficiency component of the BSER for long-term coal-fired steam generating units, finding that 90% is adequately demonstrated and technically feasible over long periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes that technology providers report solvents and process improvements achieving capture rates of 95% or greater and that minor technological improvements can help assure retrofit capture plants meet 90% capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable capture technologies and process description
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-combustion capture using liquid solvents (commonly amine-based) is an applicable capture approach for steam generating units, involving CO2 absorption into solvent, solvent regeneration by heating to release CO2, compression, pipeline transport, and geologic sequestration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA points to decades of industrial application of solvent-based capture, examples of capture at coal-fired units (e.g., Boundary Dam), and descriptions of transport and sequestration feasibility and regulation (PHMSA jurisdiction over pipelines; comprehensive regulatory structure for sequestration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation and sequestration feasibility and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 captured must be compressed and transported (generally via pipelines) to geologic sequestration sites; pipelines are subject to PHMSA safety regulations and sequestration sites are widely available across the continental U.S. with regulatory oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites thousands of miles of CO2 pipelines and tens of millions of tons of CO2 permanently stored as evidence of feasibility; sequestration has been done both for EOR and in deep saline aquifers (e.g., Aquistore).
